claim: The Moon is [386,400 km] away from Earth [01:04]
quote: The moon is 386,400 km away from Earth
evidence: NASA gives the average Earth-Moon distance as 384,400 km (perigee 363,104 km, apogee 406,696 km). The video's 386,400 km is off by ~2,000 km (0.5%) from the commonly cited average, but sits comfortably inside the Moon's real orbital range.

claim: It takes about [3 days, or 69 hours,] for a spacecraft to travel from Earth to the Moon [01:04]
quote: it takes about 3 days or 69 hours for a spacecraft to go from Earth to the moon
evidence: 69 hours matches Apollo 8 exactly (69h8m), the fastest Apollo transit. Other missions took longer: Apollo 11, 75h49m; Apollo 17 (slowest), 86h14m. 'about 3 days' is a fair summary of the range, but 69h specifically is the fast end, not the typical figure.

claim: Travelling at the speed of light, the Earth-Moon trip would take [1.3 seconds] [01:04]
quote: this trip takes a mere 1.3 seconds
evidence: Royal Museums Greenwich: light takes about 1.3 seconds Moon-to-Earth using the 384,400 km average distance. 384,400/300,000 = 1.28s ≈ 1.3s; arithmetic checks out against the standard distance figure.

claim: The speed of light is [300,000 km per second] [01:04]
quote: you'd be traveling at 300,000 km per second
evidence: c = 299,792.458 km/s; 300,000 km/s is the universally used rounded figure, off by 0.07%.

claim: The [NASA Parker Solar Probe] is the fastest human-made object ever built, reaching [635,000 km/h] [01:04]
quote: The fastest human-made object ever made is the NASA Parker Solar Probe, and that only goes a measly 635,000 km per hour
evidence: [2 URLs → 1 origin, judged: same NASA/Guinness record announcement] 635,266 km/h was PSP's Sept 2023 record. It set a newer record of 692,000 km/h on 24 Dec 2024 — public well before this video's 12 Sept 2025 publish date. The figure used is still correctly 'fastest human-made object' but understates the current record by ~9% at time of publication.

claim: As an object's speed approaches the speed of light, [its mass increases, time slows down for it, and it would take an infinite amount of energy] to reach light speed [02:08]
quote: as an object's speed gets close to the speed of light, its mass increases… time actually slows down… you'd need to have an infinite amount of energy to make this happen
evidence: DOE: relativistic mass and momentum diverge as v→c, so accelerating a massive object to light speed would require infinite energy; time dilation is a standard consequence of the same Lorentz factor. Textbook special relativity, confirmed by a government science-agency explainer.

claim: The energy released by [a needle travelling at 99.9% of the speed of light] hitting Earth would be over 100 times the energy of a nuclear bomb, [over 1 megaton of TNT] [04:16, 07:29]
quote: That's over 1 megaton of TNT
evidence: [2 URLs → 2 origins, judged] Shown sum: relativistic KE = (γ-1)mc², v=0.999c → γ=22.37. A realistic sewing needle is 0.2-1g (source: quiltnco/superiorthreads). At 0.2g: KE=3.8e14J=0.09Mt(92kt). At 1g (heavy-duty ceiling): KE=1.9e15J=0.46Mt(459kt) — both well under the claimed >1 megaton / >100x a Hiroshima-scale bomb (15kt). Reaching >1Mt requires m>2.2g, more than double the heaviest realistic sewing needle found. The claim holds only for a 'needle' far heavier than the word normally means (more like a thick skewer/rod); the video never states a mass, which is the unstated input the whole figure turns on.

claim: The energy from [the needle impact] would equal the power of an earthquake [about 7.3] on the Richter scale [04:16]
quote: equal to the power of an earthquake that's about 7.3 on the RTOR scale
evidence: Gutenberg-Richter: log10(E)=1.5M+4.8 (E in joules). For the same realistic needle mass range (0.2-1g, claim 7): M≈6.5-7.0, not 7.3. Reaching M=7.3 needs ~2.9g, the same unrealistically heavy 'needle' claim 7 needed for >1 megaton — the two figures are mutually consistent under one unstated (and oversized) mass assumption.

claim: The [1906 San Francisco] earthquake measured [7.9] on the Richter scale, destroyed over [28,000] buildings and killed more than [700] people [05:21]
quote: an earthquake that measured 7.9 on the RTER scale hit San Francisco. It destroyed over 28,000 buildings and killed more than 700 people
evidence: [2 URLs → 2 origins, judged] Magnitude 7.9 and 28,000 buildings destroyed both match USGS/Wikipedia exactly. Death toll: '>700' is technically true but is the original 1906-era undercount; USGS/modern estimates now exceed 3,000 (over 4x higher). Using the century-old low figure without the revision understates the toll.

claim: [The narrator] tried to scan an important document in bad lighting and got a blurry, unusable result [05:21]
quote: the last time I tried to scan an important document in bad lighting, ended up with a blurry, unusable mess
evidence: Personal anecdote inside a sponsor read for the iScanner app; no outside party can verify a private experience like this.

claim: [iScanner] is ranked as one of the top scanning apps worldwide with over [125 million] downloads [05:21, 06:25]
quote: ranked as one of the top scanning apps worldwide with over 125 million downloads
evidence: [2 URLs → 2 origins, judged, both tier 4] Google Play's own badge shows '100M+' downloads (store badges round down to the nearest tier); the 125M figure traces to the app's own PR and affiliate/marketing coverage, not an independent counter. A source about itself is tier 4 regardless of which outlet repeats it, so this caps at plausible, not confirmed.

claim: The [1946 Baker test] detonated a [23 kiloton] nuke underwater, creating a water plume [2 km] high and waves up to [30 m] [07:29]
quote: a 23 kiloton nuke was detonated underwater. This created a plume of water 2 km high. Waves close to the explosion radiated out at heights of up to 30 m
evidence: [2 URLs → 2 origins, judged] Yield 23kt, plume >1.3mi (~2.1km), waves up to 100ft (~30m) close to the blast all match the National Security Archive/Atomic Heritage Foundation record of the Operation Crossroads Baker test.

claim: The [2004 Indian Ocean] tsunami's earthquake was equivalent to [23,000 Hiroshima bombs] [08:34]
quote: a tsunami like the one in the Indian Ocean in 2004 which was equivalent to 23,000 Hiroshima bombs
evidence: [2 URLs → 2 origins, judged] National Geographic and World Vision both state 23,000 Hiroshima-bomb equivalent for the M9.2-9.3 Sumatra-Andaman earthquake; one outlet quotes a scientist using 40,000 with a different magnitude assumption, noted but not the majority figure.

claim: The [Toba eruption, 74,000 years ago,] almost wiped out humanity, leaving only [2,000 to 20,000] survivors [09:39]
quote: The Toba eruption 74,000 years ago almost wiped out all human beings. Only 2,000 to 20,000 humans survived that eruption and its aftermath
evidence: [2 URLs → 2 origins, judged] The Toba catastrophe hypothesis (population reduced to low thousands) is a real, decades-old proposal and the video's 2,000-20,000 range sits within the literature's historical estimates. But current research (peer-reviewed: 'Understanding the overestimated impact of the Toba super-eruption') finds no genomic evidence of the bottleneck and treats it as increasingly doubted. The video states it as settled fact with no hint it's a contested hypothesis.

claim: Volcanic ash thrown into the atmosphere can linger there for [10 years or longer], blocking the sun [10:42]
quote: Volcanic ash thrown high into the atmosphere can linger there for 10 years or longer, blocking the sun
evidence: [2 URLs → 2 origins, judged] Established estimates put volcanic-winter cooling at 1-3 years for ordinary large eruptions; even the Toba catastrophe hypothesis itself (the video's own next claim) tops out around 6 years. Most volcanic ash also settles out within weeks; it's stratospheric sulfate aerosol, not ash, that lingers. '10 years or longer' overstates every duration figure found.

claim: The current global population is [8 billion] people [11:45]
quote: our current global population of 8 billion people
evidence: World population passed 8 billion in Nov 2022 and stood at ~8.2-8.3 billion by 2025-2026; '8 billion' is the standard rounded figure used in general discourse and was true at/after the video's publish date.

claim: Spacesuit gloves allow only about [20%] of an astronaut's gloveless range of motion [12:46]
quote: spaceuit gloves that only allow about 20% of their gloveless range of motion
evidence: Peer-reviewed EVA glove study: pressurized gloves in vacuum limit hand range of motion to as little as 20% of normal range — matches exactly.

claim: The International Space Station has been continuously occupied since [the end of the year 2000] [13:49]
quote: The International Space Station has been continuously occupied since the end of the year 2000
evidence: Expedition 1 arrived 2 November 2000 and the ISS has been continuously crewed since — matches 'end of the year 2000'.

claim: Sneaking raw meat aboard the ISS would break about [20] food regulations [13:49]
quote: you would break about 20 food regulations by sneaking raw meat aboard the ISS
evidence: NASA's own food-safety documentation (room-temperature stability, HACCP process control, 6-month pre-launch approval) confirms raw meat would not be approved, but no source — after three differently-angled searches, all of which surfaced real ISS food-safety material — names a specific count of '20' regulations. The search is demonstrably working (it returns substantial on-topic results); it just never returns this number, which reads as an invented specific rather than a sourced one.

claim: The ISS orbits [400 km] above Earth [14:55]
quote: The ISS is orbiting 400 km above the Earth
evidence: NASA states the ISS orbits at about 400 km altitude (mean altitude range 370-460 km) — matches.

claim: Dropping [a steak] from [70 km] up would break the sound barrier, heating the surrounding air to [177°] for about a minute [15:58]
quote: If you drop the steak from a height of 70 km, it would break the sound barrier. For about a minute, the air around it would heat up to 177
evidence: [2 URLs → 2 origins, judged] This segment closely tracks xkcd's 'What If: Steak Drop' (Randall Munroe): its 70km figure is 'briefly exposed to 350°F air... barely lasts a minute' — 350°F=176.7°C≈177°C, matching the video almost exactly. But that same source states the sound barrier is broken by ~50km, not 70km — the video reassigns the sound-barrier threshold to the altitude it borrowed the temperature figure from.

claim: Dropping [a steak] from [100 km] up, it would fall at [twice the speed of sound] for [90 seconds] [15:58]
quote: At 100 km up, your ribeye would be falling at twice the speed of sound for 90 seconds
evidence: [2 URLs → 2 origins, judged] xkcd: 'from 100 kilometers... spends a minute and a half over Mach 2'; IFLScience's summary matches. 90 seconds at Mach 2 is exactly what the video states.

claim: Dropping [a steak] from [250 km] above Earth would sear its surface as it fell at [six times the speed of sound] [15:58-17:01]
quote: Dropping a steak down from 250 km above Earth would get it that lovely seared surface. The falling meat would travel at six times the speed of sound
evidence: [2 URLs → 2 origins, judged] xkcd: from 250km the steak reaches 'top speed of Mach 6' and the 'outer surface may even get pleasantly seared' — matches the video's six-times-the-speed-of-sound and seared-surface claims exactly. IFLScience also reports a real Mach-5 hypersonic wind-tunnel test on a steak by University of Manchester researchers confirming a seared-outside/raw-inside result.

claim: If the [ISS itself, without reboosts,] fell from orbit it would take [2.5 years] to deorbit [17:01]
quote: If the ISS itself were to fall from space, it would take 2 and 1/2 years due to the orbit it's in
evidence: NASA's own deorbit analysis puts the ISS's natural orbital lifetime without reboosts at roughly one to two years (solar-activity dependent). The video's 2.5 years is somewhat above that range but the same order of magnitude.

claim: A [steak dropped from the ISS] would go into orbit and fly back past the station roughly [90 minutes] later at about [28,000 km/h] [18:04]
quote: roughly 90 minutes later, it would be flying right back at the ISS at a speed of roughly 28,000 kmh
evidence: [2 URLs → 2 origins, judged] ISS orbital period is 92.9 minutes (≈90 min) and orbital speed is 27,600 km/h (≈28,000 km/h) — both match closely.

claim: Light can travel around the Earth [7.5 times] in a single second [00:00-01:04]
quote: it can travel around the Earth 7 and a half times in a single second
evidence: c (299,792 km/s) / Earth's equatorial circumference (40,075 km) ≈ 7.48 laps per second — matches '7 and a half times'.

claim: Astronauts have accidentally dropped items during ISS spacewalks, including [a camera] and [a spatula] [12:46-13:49]
quote: Astronauts have dropped everything from a camera to a spatula
evidence: [2 URLs → 2 origins, judged] Astronaut Piers Sellers lost a spatula during a 2006 spacewalk; cameras are also documented among items lost during EVAs (alongside the well-known 2008 and 2023 tool-bag incidents) — both specific items check out.

claim: Astronauts avoid [cabbage, beans, and broccoli] because these foods cause [flatulence], a problem in the ISS's close quarters [18:04]
quote: don't take cabbage, beans, or broccoli for a side dish. Those foods make astronauts fart, and that's never a good thing in close quarters
evidence: [2 URLs → 2 origins, judged] NASA is widely reported (NPR and others) to avoid gas-producing foods like beans, cabbage and sprouts for crew on spacecraft, citing both flammable-methane and confined-space comfort concerns — matches the claim.
